'''''Salicornia fruticosa''''', [[Synonym (taxonomy)|synonym]] '''''Sarcocornia fruticosa''''', known commonly as the '''shrubby marsh samphire''', is a species of [[Salicornia|glasswort]] in the family [[Amaranthaceae]] (pigweeds). It is native to southern Europe, north Africa, [[Western Asia]] and [[Yemen]].<ref name=POWO_1030778-2/> It is a [[halophyte]], a plant that can grow in saline conditions.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1016/j.envexpbot.2018.10.001 |title=Efficient leaf solute partioning in Salicornia fruticosa allows growth under salinity |year=2019 |last1=Marco |first1=Paula |last2=Carvajal |first2=Micaela |last3=Martínez-Ballesta |first3=María del Carmen |journal=Environmental and Experimental Botany |volume=157 |pages=177–186 |bibcode=2019EnvEB.157..177M |s2cid=92288795 }}</ref>

It is the main [[saltwort]] species used in making special [[pot ash]] made during [[Mesopotamia]]n times to the early Islamic era – قَلَيّ ''qali'' – which is the basis for the word "[[alkali]]".<ref>{{cite book|page=121|title=Chemistry and chemical technology in ancient Mesopotamia|first=Martin|last=Levey|location=Amsterdam|year=1959}}</ref>
